For the attractive logarithmic potential, we prove that the partition function is bounded uniformly in the number of particles on every compact inverse-temperature interval $[0,\be_0]$ with $\be_0<B$, where $B\in(0,2\d]$ is the sharp constant in the logarithmic Hardy–Littlewood–Sobolev inequality. The proof separates a smooth bulk, which inherits the entropy inequality, from a short-range singular interaction. The singular contribution is controlled on the event that each box of a fixed grid contains few particles. The complementary overcrowding event has exponentially small probability, which compensates a crude linear-in-$N$ bound on the log partition function. The resulting estimate supplies the partition bound that can be used recycled in a few different results. A separate Lean formalization verifies the conditional partition-bound theorem under the log-HLS assumption.

item.title: Talagrand's Convolution Bound for Tensor Powers of Finite-State Markov Semigroups
item.dc:creator: Alexander Marsh
item.description:
The main theorem, a generalization of Talagrand's convolution bound to finite-state Markov semigroups, is formally verified in Lean 4 with a public formalization produced with AI assistance.
Talagrand's convolution conjecture, recently proven by J. Lu, S. Guo, and E. Fang, concerns the smoothing properties of the heat semigroup on $\{-1,1\}^N$. We follow their perturbed coupled reverse-heat approach to generalize the theorem to tensor powers of irreducible continuous-time Markov semigroups on finite state spaces. Specifically, let $(S_t)_{t\geq0}$ be the semigroup of an irreducible continuous-time Markov chain on a finite state space $G_0$ with stationary distribution $π$. Then, for every $τ>0$, there exists a finite constant $C_{τ,S,π}<\infty$ such that, for every $N\geq1$, every nonnegative function $f:G_0^N\to[0,\infty)$, and every $η>1$, \begin{align*} π^{\otimes N}\left(S_τ^{\otimes N}f>η\int_{G_0^N}f\,dπ^{\otimes N}\right)\leq\frac{C_{τ,S,π}}{η\sqrt{\logη}}, \end{align*} where the constant is independent of $N$, $f$, and $η$. Most of the machinery developed by Lu, Guo, and Fang transfers cleanly, but since probability distributions on $|G_0|$ elements are not determined by their mean for $|G_0|>2$, we must use explicit terminal bridge laws to find a dimension-independent bound for the terminal-discrepancy estimate. We have formalized our result in Lean 4. The formalization is publicly available.

item.title: AutoAssumption: Searching over Assumptions Discovers ML-Systems Algorithms
item.dc:creator: Igor Sadalski, Minghao Guo, Benjamin Jones, Wojciech Matusik
item.description:
LLM agents formalize 89 ML-systems algorithms as Lean-checked proof graphs; variants that relax one assumption must re-prove in Lean before benchmarking.
Many advances in ML systems came from breaking an assumption that earlier methods took for granted: speculative decoding dropped the assumption that a model needs one forward pass per token. Yet algorithms rarely state their assumptions, so experts and discovery harnesses search over programs, where one edit changes several design choices and gains are difficult to attribute. Searching over the assumptions themselves remains largely unexplored. Writing algorithms as proofs makes their assumptions explicit and turns algorithm design into a search over a small, structured space that an LLM can explore and a proof checker can audit. We formalize 89 algorithms from KV-cache eviction, weight pruning and speculative decoding as proof graphs with explicit assumptions, checked in Lean. Our harness, AutoAssumption, relaxes one assumption of a published method, re-derives and re-proves it, and generates its code. In KV-cache eviction and weight pruning, this search improved on every published algorithm we ran and produced state-of-the-art algorithms. The eviction algorithm has the highest RULER-4K score of the published methods we ran, and the pruning algorithm the lowest perplexity of thirteen on four LLaMA models. At equal budget, the harness scores within a point of OpenEvolve, an open-source implementation of AlphaEvolve, with a lower standard deviation across repeats. Future work will formalize more fields and combine them through the principal assumptions they share.

item.title: Stability of equilibria in discrete-time modified-gradient systems and the multivariate breeder's equation
item.dc:creator: Benjamin J. Ridenhour
item.description:
The main lemma, stability theorems, corollary, and basin-of-attraction theorem are machine-checked in Lean 4 with Mathlib, with a public GitHub/Zenodo artifact.
The multivariate breeder's equation $Δ ar z=G
abla\ln ar W$ is a widely used discrete-time modified-gradient system describing the evolution of continuous traits in organisms. This system could more conventionally be expressed as $x_{k+1}=x_k+P_k
abla f(x_k)$. For its continuous-time counterpart $x'=P(t)
abla f(x)$, it has been proven that an isolated local maximum of $f$ is uniformly stable whenever $P(t)$ is positive semidefinite, as is the case for the "$G$-matrix." Furthermore, the continuous time system is uniformly asymptotically stable when the maximum is an isolated critical point and $\int_0^\inftyλ_1(P(t))\,dt=\infty$. We show that the literal discrete analog of this result is false: with constant positive definite $P$ the iterates can oscillate or diverge. The result is restored by a single additional hypothesis, a uniform bound on the largest eigenvalue of $P_k$, $λ_n$, such that $λ_n(P_k)\le 2/L$ where $L$ is a local Lipschitz constant of $
abla f$. Under this bound the maximum is uniformly stable; under a stricter version together with $\sum_kλ_1(P_k)=\infty$, the maximum is uniformly asymptotically stable. Given these hypotheses, a level-set estimate of the basin of attraction carries over. Both bounds are sharp, and each remaining hypothesis is shown to be necessary. Biologically, the bound says that genetic variance in every direction must be small relative to the curvature of log mean fitness; outside this regime the mean phenotype can overshoot a fitness peak as hypothesized by Fisher's geometric model. As further application of our results, the same conditions apply to the mean update of Gaussian evolutionary optimization algorithms, in which the covariance of the search population plays the role of $G$.

item.title: What the occupation law of a finite Markov chain determines: time reversal and principal minors
item.dc:creator: Arjun Pemmasani
item.description:
Finite and algebraic proof steps are formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib in ancillary files, assuming a Perron–Frobenius null-vector hypothesis; the Lean code was AI-generated.
What does the occupation law of a finite Markov chain determine about its generator $Q$? From the stationary start, the law of the occupation times at one time determines $Q$ exactly up to time reversal and reversals of memoryless blocks, the sets of states that are all left at one rate with one landing law and are entered in proportion to the stationary law. These reversals commute and give exactly $2^k$ generators, with $k$ read off a tree of memoryless blocks. This leaves only time reversal when $Q$ has no rank-one cut, when there are at most 4 states, and generically. The law at one time determines the law at every time, and a generic start determines $Q$. A renewal block is a set of states that is left at the same rates from each of its states, is entered with one law, and is charged by the start in proportion to that law. From every start the law determines $Q$ exactly up to lumped reversals, which lump disjoint renewal blocks to single states and reverse a memoryless block of the lumped chain. We also find every start that hides time reversal. At the scale of large deviations, the functional of Donsker and Varadhan determines exactly the principal minors of $-Q$.

item.title: Finite-Cadence Refresh Equilibria for Streaming Prior-Anchored Ridge: A Closed-Form Forgetting Window and Spectral Correction
item.dc:creator: Mrigank Shekhar Singh
item.description:
The algebraic core, refresh-chain recursion, OGD/Hedge regret bounds, and coupled contraction are formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib: 85 declarations, no sorry.
Recursive estimators on drifting streams must forget stale data fast enough to track the target, yet slowly enough to average out noise. In prior-anchored ridge regression, this trade-off admits a closed-form spectral decomposition in which each eigen-direction interpolates between the data solution and the prior with pull weight $s_i = ρ/ (μ_i + ρ)$. When the anchor is refreshed every $k$ steps, we show that the moving-frame offset converges to a finite-cadence equilibrium that lags the pure-leaky path by an explicit $Δ_k(s)$ while reducing estimation variance by a factor $Ψ(s, r_k)$. Minimizing the cycle-averaged risk gives $ω^* = (4ν^2 Σ/ c')^{1/3}$, $c' = σ^2 d_{\mathrm{eff}}(ρ)$, and the plug-in strength $ρ^* = σ^2 / (nδ^2)$. A random-matrix deterministic equivalent extends both laws to finite dimension, renormalizing the anchor to $ρ_{\mathrm{eff}} = ρ(e^{ζq} - 1) / (ζq)$; it matches simulation within 5% at fixed operating points and within 13% at the method's own, and rank-deficient populations reduce exactly to their active subspace. The resulting method, SPAR, calibrates window and strength online from residuals. On a 27-configuration grid the calibrated window opens on drift without divergence, and the grid defaults transfer to an hourly electricity stream and to BCI IV 2b. The core algebra, refresh chain, and regret bounds are formalized in Lean 4.

item.title: The bias interval of the elephant random walk
item.dc:creator: Arjun Pemmasani
item.description:
A public repository provides Lean files that machine-check the finite sign-change arguments and the analytic threshold proof, taking the classical weak limit as a hypothesis.
Guérin, Laulin, Raschel, and Simon conjectured that the initial biases giving the superdiffusive elephant random walk a bimodal limit law form an interval centered at one half, and they described the problem as challenging. We prove this. For every superdiffusive memory, strongly biased starts are unimodal, and the limit density has two local maxima exactly when the bias lies in a proper open interval. Outside it, including its endpoints, the density has a unique local maximum. The interval is nonempty exactly above a single memory threshold, numerically about $0.6688$, whose uniqueness follows from a positive-weight integral for the central curvature of the fair-start density. We control sign changes in the finite walk's first and second differences, including those created at the boundary, and pass them to the limit. The bias boundary is continuous and tends to zero at least quadratically fast as memory tends to one.

item.title: Wolfe's Minimum-Norm-Point Method Generalizes the Simplex Method
item.dc:creator: Yann Disser, Nils Mosis
item.description:
The main theorem, corollaries and all numbered supporting statements were formally verified in Lean 4, with the artifact archived on Zenodo.
Wolfe's method computes the point of minimum Euclidean norm in the convex hull of finitely many points. The method is parameterized by an insertion rule and it has been an open problem whether Wolfe's original rule guarantees a polynomial number of iterations (De Loera, Haddock, and Rademacher; STOC'18). We resolve this question by proving an exponential lower bound. In fact, we establish a tight connection to the simplex method for linear programming that allows us to transfer many lower bounds for simplex pivot rules to corresponding insertion rules of Wolfe's method. These include not only Wolfe's linopt rule via Dantzig's pivot rule, but also many other classical, randomized and history-based rules. As a corollary, we obtain the first exponential example for the Lawson-Hanson algorithm for nonnegative least squares, as well as PSPACE-hardness of deciding whether the linopt rule ever uses a given point.

item.title: More particles or the pair? An exact test of how to improve mode-coupling theory
item.dc:creator: Hu Cang
item.description:
Finite-order bounds and a factorial estimate for the generalized mode-coupling hierarchy are proved as machine-checked theorems in Lean 4.
How a dense liquid arrests into a glass remains a central problem in physics. Mode-coupling theory (MCT), the leading microscopic theory of the glass transition, fails to reproduce mean-field caging. Two routes are proposed to repair it: tracking more-particle correlations, or enforcing repulsion within each colliding pair. Testing both on an exact benchmark liquid, we show that MCT lets touching spheres pass through each other at all orders: adding particles dilutes memory and worsens the transition, whereas restoring pair impenetrability recovers mean-field arrest and the cage size.
